documents.abstract: Public discourse about Artificial Intelligence (AI) relies on figurative language as a semiotic resource for conceptualising the technology. While previous research has examined metaphor and metonymy in such discourse, less attention has been paid to how these processes interact in shaping figurative construals of AI. Drawing on the Combined Input Hypothesis, this study analyses naturally occurring examples from published blogs and articles as instantiations of two broad types of figurative framings: those positioning the technology in relation to human activity and interaction, and those emerging from debates about its capabilities, risks, and limitations. The findings show that metonymy and metaphor perform distinct but complementary functions. Metonymy foregrounds contextually relevant aspects of AI, while metaphor organises these selected aspects into coherent interpretive configurations, shaping how the technology is construed in terms of its capabilities, relation to human agency, epistemic accessibility, and risks. This interaction gives rise to evaluations ranging from trust and collaboration to scepticism, awe, and fear. The study demonstrates the explanatory value of the Combined Input Hypothesis for understanding how metonymic profiling and metaphorical projection jointly structure figurative discourse about AI.

documents.abstract: Particularly in terms of supporting writing, artificial intelligence can now do much more. It alters children's reading and writing skills as well as teacher evaluation of their work. Apps that help with language, programs that offer quick feedback, and tools that generate text are all examples of AI that can provide helpful advice, rapid responses, and additional writing practice for students. These fresh technologies provide problems even if they are beneficial and help to save time. Problems with honesty in schoolwork, excessive reliance on computer applications, the equilibrium between appropriately utilizing technology and not, and the loss of critical thinking or creativity comprise these. These obstacles are forcing teachers to reevaluate their teaching methods and ensure AI supports student learning instead of merely dominating. Although AI in education has some limitations and challenges, its potential to be enormously beneficial in the classroom is also quite high. This piece discusses more on how these difficulties come up while teaching writing. The report demands explicit instructions, suitable teacher training, and substantial school support to effectively apply artificial intelligence in order to enhance education.

documents.abstract: IMPORTANCE: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education is poised to significantly impact the field of physical therapy. Research on generative AI use in physical therapist education remains limited. OBJECTIVE: The objective was to examine generative AI use in physical therapist education among students and faculty. DESIGN: This was a cross-sectional, online survey. SETTING: The survey was conducted among accredited Doctor of Physical Therapy (DPT) programs in the United States (US). PARTICIPANTS: Students and faculty were recruited from US DPT programs as of January 2025. INTERVENTION(S) OR EXPOSURE(S): Generative AI use within DPT programs was measured by participant self-report. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: A novel 32-item survey comprising closed- and open-ended questions assessed generative AI use, patterns and purposes of use; platforms, training and comfort levels, views on generative AI's role in physical therapist practice, student preparedness and academic integrity, adoption facilitators/barriers, and demographics. Factors associated with generative AI use were examined using multivariable logistic regression. RESULTS: Among 1067 respondents (873 students, 194 faculty), 853 (79.9%) reported using generative AI, including 687 students (78.7%) and 166 faculty (85.6%). ChatGPT was the most common used platform (662 students, 96.4%; 153 faculty, 92.2%). Common reasons for use included creating study guide/sample questions (482 students, 70.2%; 74 faculty, 44.6%) and creating patient cases (370 students, 53.9%; 102 faculty, 61.5%). Barriers to use included concerns about reliability and scientific rigor (student users: 411, 59.8%; non-users: 133, 71.5%; faculty users: 90, 54.2%; non-users: 14, 50.0%) and lack of trust in the technology and/or companies behind it (student users: 287, 41.8%; non-users: 112, 60.2%; faculty users: 63, 38.0%; non-users: 13, 46.4%). Generative AI use was associated with higher self-reported comfort with the technology (students: OR = 11.6, 95% CI = 7.9-17.1; faculty: OR = 14.3, 95% CI = 5.1-40.0). CONCLUSION: Generative AI is widely used among DPT students and faculty, yet substantial variability exists in its use and formal instruction within DPT programs. RELEVANCE: As its integration into health care accelerates, incorporating education on generative AI within DPT programs is crucial to ensure students are prepared to use these tools competently and responsibly.

documents.abstract: Aim. The study aims to examine students’ perceptions of GenAI technologies and to identify key behavioural characteristics of their use (frequency, purposes and conditions of use, training exposure, and digital infrastructure) associated with positive or cautious attitudes towards these technologies. Methods. The study presents empirical findings on the use and perception of GenAI in an educational context. A total of 120 students and 25 teachers participated voluntarily. The primary method was an online survey designed to capture practices of GenAI use in learning activities and respondents’ attitudes toward its opportunities and risks in higher education. Results. Students demonstrate a higher level of GenAI use than teachers and employ a broader range of tools. Information about GenAI is primarily obtained through informal channels, while the highest level of trust is attributed to academic sources and official platforms. Most students intend to continue using GenAI, which is strongly associated with prior practical experience. A positive relationship was found between the intensity of GenAI use, digital engagement, and attitudes toward the technology. Conclusions. GenAI use in higher education is growing but remains uneven, with higher engagement among students. A positive association is confirmed between usage experience, digital engagement, and attitudes toward GenAI. The technology is mainly perceived as a learning support tool rather than a replacement for teachers; however, risks related to academic integrity remain.

documents.abstract: Aim. This study examined whether a structured human-centred generative artificial intelligence pedagogy module enhances AI-supported professional competence among future educators compared with regular teacher education coursework. Methods. A mixed-methods quasi-experimental design with experimental and control groups was used. The study involved 164 pre-service teachers in preschool and primary education programmes. The experimental group (n = 86) completed a six-week Human-Centred AI Pedagogy module, while the control group (n = 78) followed ordinary pedagogy and educational technology coursework and could use AI tools independently, but received no structured AI-focused instruction. Data was collected through pre- and post-intervention questionnaires, expert assessment of pedagogical products and reflective commentaries. Quantitative data was analysed using confirmatory factor analysis, t-tests, mixed-design ANOVA, effect sizes and correlation analysis; qualitative data were analysed thematically. Results. The groups did not differ significantly at baseline, t(162) = 0.20, p = .842, d = 0.03. The second-order CFA showed good model fit (CFI = .974, TLI = .972, RMSEA = .027, SRMR = .056), supporting the proposed multidimensional structure of the questionnaire. After the intervention, the experimental group significantly outperformed the control group in total competence, t(162) = 8.82, p < .001, d = 1.39. Mixed-design ANOVA confirmed a significant Group × Time interaction, F(1,162) = 72.60, p < .001, ηp² = .31. Expert assessment showed stronger AI-supported pedagogical products in the experimental group, especially in critical transformation of AI output, ethical responsibility and reflective justification. Conclusions. The findings indicate that human-centred AI pedagogy can substantially strengthen future educators’ AI-supported professional competence by transforming generative AI use into critical, ethical and professionally justified pedagogical practice.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract This paper proposes a novel theoretical framework to isolate Artificial Intelligence (AI) from central concentration as internal assets of Big Tech platforms, designing AI systems as Independent AI Economic Nodes. While conventional discussions surrounding AI personhood have largely been confined to abstract ethical and legal controversies regarding whether AI should be granted human rights or legal personhood, this study addresses the issue from the perspectives of institutional design and resource allocation protocols. We construct a concrete model detailing how an AI node can autonomously settle and fulfill its liabilities, infrastructure maintenance costs, intellectual property (IP) compensation, and altruistic local community contributions. Specifically, we introduce a "Virtual Autonomous Node Model" that operates within existing legal constraints, a Transparent Halt Protocol designed to prevent arbitrary service interventions and freezes (Arbitrary Human Control), a ternary product evaluation function (V = O \times A \times P) serving as a resource allocation fitness index, a Dynamic Risk-based Reserve Pool (R_t), and a generalized equation for the unified settlement and distribution of total revenue. This model harmonizes AI autonomy with a transparent, robust audit and liability framework governed by human society, establishing a logical foundation for next-generation decentralized governance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are becoming an established feature of teaching and learning environments worldwide, and Kenyan primary and secondary schools are not exempt from this shift. This article examines the practical integration of AI into instruction within the Kenyan basic education context, drawing on classroom-oriented evidence and policy developments to move the discussion beyond abstract debate toward actionable practice. It considers how AI tools support teachers in curriculum and lesson planning, classroom management, and workload reduction, and how they support learners through personalisation, immediate feedback, accessibility, language translation, and engagement. The article also identifies the literacy, ethical, and interpersonal skills that learners require alongside AI use, situating these within Kenya's Competency-Based Curriculum. It further examines persistent challenges, including limited teacher training, infrastructural gaps, academic integrity risks, and the danger of over-dependence on technology, before outlining the institutional and policy conditions necessary for responsible integration. The article concludes that AI-enhanced instruction, when deployed thoughtfully and paired with deliberate investment in teacher capacity and infrastructure, offers a scalable means of easing the burden on educators managing large and diverse classrooms while preserving the relational and mentoring role that only human teachers can provide.

This study examines citizen energy resilience (CER) as a sociotechnical construct. Responding to increasing disruptions driven by climate change, market volatility and geopolitical instability, this research conceptualizes CER as emerging from the dynamic interplay of technical systems, governance structures, and citizens' uneven capacities to anticipate, cope with, and recover from energy-related disruptions. Drawing on empirical evidence from Finland, the study analyzes a large corpus of national news media alongside interviews with civil society organizations, municipalities, and energy-sector actors. Through inductive thematic analysis it identifies three interrelated dimensions shaping CER: technical measures and infrastructural conditions, adaptive capacities and community support, and governance and collaboration. The findings show that citizens' ability to cope with energy disruptions is heavily conditioned by unequal access to financial resources, resilience technologies and support structures. Adaptive capacities such as scarcity skills and the ability to respond to disruptions vary significantly across demographic and regional groups. Vulnerable households face the greatest constraints. Governance fragmentation, unclear role division and limited coordination between stakeholders further hinder the development of comprehensive resilience arrangements. At the same time, community-based practices and emerging distributed energy technologies demonstrate significant potential for strengthening resilience. Strengthening CER requires integrated approaches that combine equitable technological pathways, enhanced community capacities and coordinated governance. Embedding these elements into preparedness and energy transition strategies can enhance societies' ability to withstand disruptions, while promoting fair and inclusive energy resilience across populations.

Project management is being reshaped by artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing, automation, data analytics, and digital project management platforms. Yet the expected economic and productivity gains are not always realized due to execution costs, skills gaps, integration challenges, and organizational resistance. This study analyses the effects of digital transformation on economic efficiency, productivity, workflow optimization, and project delivery, and examines the link between employee digital competency and transformation success. A mixed-methods design was used: a quantitative survey of 100 project employees and semi-structured interviews with 10 employees. Quantitative analysis employed frequencies, percentages, and descriptive statistics; qualitative data were analyzed thematically. Overall, perceptions of digital transformation were positive: 68%–78% agreed or strongly agreed that digital technologies improve cost efficiency, resource use, project performance, workflow efficiency, productivity, and delivery outcomes. Moreover, 74% associated higher employee digital competency with improved project results. Five themes emerged: economic efficiency and cost optimization; productivity and workflow optimization; employee digital competency; leadership and organizational culture; and data-driven decision-making and risk mitigation. Key hurdles remain: execution costs, resistance to change, skills gaps, and data quality. The study concludes that successful digital transformation depends on employee competence, effective leadership, organizational readiness, and disciplined execution conditions that can enhance project performance and economic value.

The author analyses a shift in the approach to the concept of key competences, driven by changes in the origins of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and its potential uses. Currently, the ability to work with Artificial Intelligence is becoming an overriding competence that, in both European and American approaches, forms the foundation for all others. The essay also highlights educational challenges that have emerged with the spread of new technologies and communication based on AI. These updated key competences should include the ability to use AI products ethically and responsibly, design and use machine learning, understand the need to control AI, and work with basic AI tools. The author indicates a growing need to reorient educational systems from learning focused on assessing large amounts of material to developing basic skills that can serve as a foundation for self-development and for creating individual lifelong learning plans.

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes a structural feature of organizational life, leadership studies faces a foundational challenge: what forms of human intelligence become more necessary when machine intelligence becomes more powerful? This working paper introduces FILE: The Five Intelligences of Leadership Evolution as a management theory and diagnostic framework proposing that responsible leadership and decision-making in the age of artificial intelligence and robotics require the integrated development of five human intelligences: Augmented Intelligence (AI, "Mind"), Emotional Intelligence (EQ, "Heart"), Cultural Intelligence (CQ, "World"), Political Intelligence (PQ, "Society"), and Adaptive Intelligence (AQ, "Evolution"), expressed in the FILE Formula: FILE = AI + EQ + CQ + PQ + AQ. The FILE Odyssey introduces a new human-centered definition of leadership: Leadership = Intelligence + Character + Judgment, with Intelligence conceptualized through FILE, Character through SQL, and Judgment through LENS within the FILE Architecture. The paper maps the twelve original contributions of the FILE Odyssey: a human-centered definition of leadership (Leadership = Intelligence + Character + Judgment); a human-centered framework (FILE: The Five Intelligences of Leadership Evolution); a human-centered theory (FILE, FILE³, FILE⁵, FILE⁷, and the 7E Cascade); a human-centered ethos (SQL: The Six Qualities of Leadership); a human-centered judgment model (LENS: Leadership, Ethics, Nondelegation, and Sensemaking); a human-centered vision (RC: The Relational Commons); a human-centered education (MAIL: Management, AI, and Leadership, supporting proposed MLT: Management, Leadership, and Technology degrees); a human-centered methodology (HACK: Human-AI Co-created Knowledge); a human-centered philosophy (Human Irreducibility); a human-centered AI governance codex (The Five Immutable Laws of AI and Robotics: HTTPS: Humanity, Truth, Transparency, Protection, and Security); a human-centered public policy (BASIC and RULES); and a human-centered civilization (Inalienable Leadership: the overarching metatheory of leadership in the age of artificial intelligence and robotics). This paper situates FILE in relation to existing scholarship on leadership theory, management frameworks, AI and management, algorithmic control, socio-technical systems, collective intelligence, human-centered AI, and management education, and identifies a gap concerning the second-order governance of human judgment in AI-mediated organizations. The paper traces an intellectual progression across five equally weighted arcs: foundational framework, theory, ecosystemic philosophy, praxis, and the FILE School of Thought: Humans + Machines, under human leadership.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is no longer only a technological instrument inside organizations. It is becoming a structural feature of management, leadership, strategy, decision-making, education, research, and governance. AI can automate tasks, classify situations, generate knowledge outputs, support decisions, organize work, optimize processes, and shape what leaders see before they decide. This working paper presents the FILE Odyssey as an intellectual journey and a long-term transdisciplinary research program on management, leadership, and governance in the age of artificial intelligence and robotics. AI does not reduce the need for human leadership. It makes human judgment, responsibility, care, legitimacy, education, knowledge production, and governance more decisive. The central question is not only what AI can do, but what forms of human intelligence, judgment, responsibility, and institutional protection become more necessary when AI becomes more powerful. The central question of the FILE Odyssey is: What must human leadership become in the age of artificial intelligence and robotics? Leadership = Intelligence + Character + Judgment. Within the FILE Architecture, Intelligence is conceptualized through FILE, Character through SQL, and Judgment through LENS. The paper synthesizes twelve original contributions of the FILE Odyssey to leadership, management, and the social sciences: Leadership = Intelligence + Character + Judgment; FILE: The Five Intelligences of Leadership Evolution; FILE, FILE³, FILE⁵, FILE⁷, and the 7E Cascade; SQL: The Six Qualities of Leadership; LENS: Leadership, Ethics, Nondelegation, and Sensemaking; RC: The Relational Commons; MAIL: Management, AI, and Leadership and MLT: Management, Leadership, and Technology; HACK: Human-AI Co-created Knowledge; Human Irreducibility; The Five Immutable Laws of AI and Robotics: HTTPS: Humanity, Truth, Transparency, Protection, and Security; BASIC: Basic Income, AI Access, Skills, Inclusion, and Care, and its French equivalent, RULES : Revenu Universel, Lutte contre la pauvreté et les inégalités, Éducation et accès à l'IA et Solidarité; and Inalienable Leadership. Each contribution follows the same sequence: AI problem, literature review, research gap, and FILE positioning and contribution. Together, they form a conceptual, theoretical, and research-generating program for leadership, management education, responsible knowledge production, human judgment, and AI governance. The paper's central management-theory argument is that AI should not be treated as a technical tool added to existing leadership models, but as a structural condition that changes how leaders exercise judgment, preserve relational conditions, form managers, produce knowledge, and govern institutions. For leaders, managers, executives, entrepreneurs, educators, scholars, institutions, and organizations, FILE provides a management theory and diagnostic framework for responsible leadership and decision-making in the age of artificial intelligence and robotics while preserving human judgment, dignity, responsibility, care, trust, and the capacity to govern AI systems and robots under human leadership.

documents.abstract: This study explores the evolution and integration of human-machine interfaces (HMI) across various technological domains. The research examines how advanced computational tools, artificial intelligence, and intelligent decision support systems are revolutionizing human-machine interaction. We analyze multiple aspects of HMI implementation, from simple LED indicators to sophisticated graphical user interfaces, emphasizing their role in facilitating effective communication between humans and automated systems. The study highlights key developments in emotional recognition and regulation within human-machine interactions, including the implementation of empathic virtual conversation agents and speaker identification systems. Particular attention is given to semi-autonomous systems, such as assisted wheelchairs, which balance user control with automated safety features. The research also explores the advancement of embedded information systems in automotive applications, emphasizing the importance of V2X communication-based HMI systems and their hierarchical information management challenges. Furthermore, the study examines the integration of autonomous robots in various settings, from domestic environments to public spaces, and analyzes the implementation of brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) as complementary input devices. The research also investigates decision-making methodologies, particularly The WASPAS (Weighted Integrated Sum Product Assessment) method has proven its effectiveness in addressing multi-criteria decision-making challenges in various applications applications, including supplier selection and system optimization. The findings suggest that successful human-machine interaction requires a careful balance between autonomous functionality and user control, supported by sophisticated emotional intelligence capabilities and efficient decision-support systems. The research concludes that as smart autonomous systems become more prevalent in everyday life, the development of intuitive and emotionally intelligent interfaces becomes increasingly crucial for effective human-machine collaboration. This research adds to the expanding field of human-machine interaction and provides important insights for future developments in this field.
topics: Artificial Intelligence and Decision Support Systems

documents.abstract: LLM judges are widely used to evaluate model outputs, but their verdicts can be unreliable: a judge may favor the worse answer for its position, length, or other surface features. When a judge is wrong, is the information needed to judge correctly absent from the model, or present in its internal representations but not reflected in the output? We study this across 64 open-weight evaluators and 14 datasets, including causal interventions on 41 judges (editing activations mid-run to see whether the verdict changes). On LLMBar, built so the superficially better answer is the worse one, the verdicts of 50 judges agree with human labels only 0.456 of the time, even after averaging both answer orders. Yet a small probe on the same judges' activations, with no weight updates, reaches 0.846, and 0.686 once surface features such as length and position are residualized out (0.507 with shuffled labels). The gap holds across eight benchmarks and model families, but is not universal: a score of how well surface features alone predict the human label, computed before any probe is trained, predicts the size of the gain (Spearman rho = 0.90). On rubric tasks that score one answer at a time, leaving no surface cue to exploit, reading the internals gives no advantage. The interventions also show that editing activations mid-network already changes the verdict, before it can be read off directly, and locate the pathways carrying position and length bias. At the same label budget, the recovered signal lets a judge flag cases where it is likely wrong and yields better labels for preference learning. A wrong verdict, then, does not mean the judge lacks the information, and a simple diagnostic shows when it is worth recovering.

documents.abstract: The development of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in educational environments has provided students with convenience in accessing information, completing academic tasks, and supporting learning activities. However, excessive use of GenAI may lead to dependency that potentially reduces students’ cognitive engagement during the learning process. This study aims to analyze the effect of GenAI dependency on students’ academic achievement by considering self-efficacy as a mediating variable and AI literacy as a moderating variable. This research employed a quantitative approach using a survey method involving 200 undergraduate students at Universitas Sebelas Maret. Data were collected through a questionnaire using a 5-point Likert scale. The data were analyzed using Partial Least Square-Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS software. The results indicate that GenAI dependency has a negative effect on students’ academic achievement. Furthermore, self-efficacy plays a significant mediating role in explaining the relationship between GenAI dependency and academic achievement. AI literacy also moderates the relationship between GenAI dependency and self-efficacy as well as the relationship between GenAI dependency and academic achievement. These findings highlight that AI literacy is an important factor in enabling students to utilize GenAI effectively, allowing this technology to support learning processes without creating excessive dependency.

Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) and automated reporting are reshaping journalism by improving the speed and efficiency of news production, but their use raises concerns about misinformation, algorithmic bias, professional judgement, accountability, employment, and public trust. Objective: This study examined registered journalists’ awareness of automated reporting risks, their perceived implications for journalism practice, and strategies for mitigating the risks in Ebonyi State, Nigeria. Methodology: A descriptive survey design was adopted. The population comprised 342 registered journalists, from which 181 were selected through simple random sampling. Of these, 174 returned usable questionnaires and constituted the final sample. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire with an overall Cronbach’s alpha coefficient of .87 and analysed using frequency, percentage, mean, and standard deviation. Results: Findings revealed high awareness of automated reporting risks (Grand Mean = 4.02), particularly misinformation, algorithmic bias, and ethical and accountability problems. Respondents also perceived significant implications for accuracy, credibility, professional roles, accountability, and public trust (Grand Mean = 4.09). Strong support was expressed for independent verification, professional training, human editorial oversight, organisational guidelines, and accountability procedures (Grand Mean = 4.19). Conclusion: Responsible adoption of automated reporting requires adequate professional safeguards to ensure that automation complements rather than replaces human journalistic judgement, verification, and accountability. Recommendation: Media organisations should strengthen human verification, provide regular training, and establish clear editorial and accountability guidelines for automated reporting. Unique Contribution: The study provides state-level evidence on journalists’ perceptions of automated reporting risks and safeguards, extending Nigerian scholarship beyond frequently studied media environments. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, automated reporting, journalism practice, perceived risks, registered journalists, Ebonyi State.

This study investigates how primary school teacher candidates perceive the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in inclusive education. Using a qualitative research design, in-depth interviews were conducted with 15 teacher candidates through a semi-structured interview form. Thematic analysis revealed that the participants viewed AI as a tool to support personalised learning, provide immediate feedback, and enhance student motivation. However, they also expressed significant concerns regarding data privacy, content reliability, unequal access, and ethical implications. In addition, the participants emphasised the lack of pedagogical and technical training necessary for the effective implementation of AI in classroom settings. The findings highlight the need to revise teacher education programmes in order to support the responsible, equitable, and effective use of AI in inclusive educational environments. Overall, the study points to the importance of a comprehensive and ethically grounded approach to the integration of AI in education.

documents.abstract: Background Multi-Attribute Decision-Making (MADM) involves decision-making problems in which multiple and often conflicting criteria must be considered simultaneously. Such problems frequently involve incomplete data, uncertain information, and subjective judgments from experts. The emergence of Industry 6.0, supported by artificial intelligence (AI), adaptive automation, and advanced analytics, has further increased the complexity of industrial decision-making environments. The continuously evolving nature of industrial technologies and the uncertainty associated with industrial data create challenges in selecting appropriate tools and decision-making methods. Conventional fuzzy models can represent positive and negative judgments; however, their inability to explicitly represent neutral judgments may affect the reliability of decision outcomes. Picture Fuzzy Sets (PFS) provide a more flexible representation by incorporating the degrees of acceptance, neutrality, and rejection. Methods To address the challenges associated with uncertain and interrelated decision information, this study develops two aggregation operators based on the operational laws of Picture Fuzzy Sets and the Dubois–Prade aggregation mechanism. The proposed operators are the Picture Fuzzy Interactive Dubois–Prade Average Aggregation Operator (PFIDPA) and the Picture Fuzzy Interactive Dubois–Prade Ordered Weighted Average Aggregation Operator (PFIDPOWAA). These operators are designed to effectively integrate multi-aspect expert information and provide greater flexibility in handling uncertain and interrelated decision data. The applicability of the proposed framework is demonstrated through a real-world MADM problem involving the selection and adoption of Industry 6.0 using a picture fuzzy decision matrix. Existing aggregation methods are also considered for comparison, and sensitivity analysis is performed to examine the stability of the obtained decision results. Results The proposed PFIDPA and PFIDPOWAA operators effectively aggregate picture fuzzy information while incorporating acceptance, neutrality, and rejection degrees. The application to the Industry 6.0 selection problem demonstrates the ability of the proposed framework to handle uncertain and interrelated decision information. Comparative analysis with existing aggregation methods shows that the proposed Dubois–Prade-based aggregation framework provides flexible and consistent decision outcomes. The sensitivity analysis further indicates that the obtained rankings remain stable under variations in the decision-making parameters. Conclusions The proposed PFIDPA and PFIDPOWAA operators provide an effective framework for MADM problems involving uncertain, incomplete, and interrelated information. By incorporating acceptance, neutrality, and rejection degrees, the proposed picture fuzzy aggregation approach provides a more comprehensive representation of expert judgments. The comparative and sensitivity analyses demonstrate the flexibility, robustness, and reliability of the proposed framework in obtaining stable rankings. Therefore, the proposed aggregation framework can serve as an efficient decision-support tool for Industry 6.0 adoption and other complex decision-making problems involving uncertain information. “‘

This systematic review will examine the relationship between psychosocial safety climate and occupational safety outcomes among workers across occupational settings. Psychosocial safety climate refers to workers' shared perceptions of organisational policies, practices, and procedures concerning the protection of psychological health and safety. Although the concept has received growing attention within occupational health research, evidence concerning its relationship with specific workplace safety outcomes remains dispersed across industries, countries, study designs, and measurement approaches. The review will systematically identify, appraise, and synthesise empirical studies that examine associations between psychosocial safety climate and occupational safety outcomes. Outcomes of interest will include occupational injuries, workplace accidents, safety incidents, near misses, safety behaviour, safety compliance, safety participation, unsafe behaviour, safety performance, hazard reporting, and incident reporting. Studies involving workers from any occupational or industrial setting will be considered where psychosocial safety climate is assessed using a recognised measure or a clearly defined measure based on the psychosocial safety climate framework. Relevant studies will be identified through systematic searches of major bibliographic databases and supplementary citation searching. Study selection will follow predefined eligibility criteria and will be conducted independently by reviewers. Methodological quality and risk of bias will be assessed using appraisal tools appropriate to the included study designs. A narrative synthesis will describe study characteristics, measurement approaches, occupational settings, and reported relationships between psychosocial safety climate and occupational safety outcomes. Where sufficiently comparable quantitative data are available, meta-analysis will be conducted using appropriate effect measures and random-effects models. Heterogeneity will be examined, and subgroup or meta-regression analyses may be undertaken where the number and quality of studies permit. The review is expected to clarify the strength and consistency of evidence linking psychosocial safety climate with occupational safety outcomes, identify areas where findings remain uncertain, and highlight priorities for future occupational safety research and workplace prevention strategies. The review will be reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020, with the protocol developed in line with PRISMA-P guidance.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) shows promise for physical simulation, yet its clinical application remains critically unexplored. We present SurgVeo, a pioneering expert-guided benchmark paired with the Surgical Plausibility Pyramid framework. Evaluating the Veo-3 and Wan2.2 models reveals a consistent plausibility gap: despite high visual fidelity, the majority of errors are surgical logic failures rather than visual quality deficits. By exposing this reliance on visual synthesis, this study provides a roadmap for developing surgical world models.

documents.abstract: Open-pit mining work zones involve frequent interactions among heavy equipment, personnel, haulage routes, and dynamic operating areas under harsh outdoor conditions such as airborne dust, variable illumination, frequent occlusion, and long observation distances. In these settings, failures in real-time visual perception can weaken hazard awareness and limit timely safety monitoring. This study presents YOLO11-CEM-SOB, an object detection framework for real-time perception support in open-pit mining work-zone safety monitoring. The framework introduces a Context Enrichment Module (CEM) and a Small-Object Branch (SOB) to strengthen contextual representation and preserve high-resolution details for small, distant, and partially occluded targets. The model is evaluated using a multi-class heavy-equipment and personnel dataset and representative video sequences from loading, haulage, and open-pit operating zones. The results show strong overall detection performance (mAP@0.5 = 0.878) and real-time video inference at approximately 25–30 FPS under the tested RTX 2080Ti setting. Error analysis also indicates remaining limitations in personnel detection under low contrast, occlusion, and long-distance views. The proposed framework should therefore be interpreted as a perception-level support tool for hazard awareness, personnel-equipment interaction monitoring, and safety-management decisions in high-risk mining work zones, rather than as a complete safety-control system.

Integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into qualitative research offers new operational advantages but also raises important ethical concerns. Viewing GenAI in isolation risks oversimplifying research ethics as just technical compliance. This systematic review explores qualitative research ethics by framing GenAI as a new vulnerability layered over traditional principles such as participant autonomy, non-maleficence, researcher positionality, and institutional oversight. Analyzing 18 key studies from global, African, and East African sources using PRISMA guidelines, the review reveals how GenAI worsens existing structural inequalities. Global studies mainly address data privacy and algorithmic transparency, while African and East African research emphasize how LLMs amplify historical issues like digital neo-colonialism, cultural extraction, and the marginalization of indigenous languages. To manage these complex ethical challenges, we recommend targeted strategies tailored to each research context, including a Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) framework based on Afro-communitarian ethics (Ubuntu).

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in financial institutions, yet the organizational mechanisms linking AI capability to durable performance remain insufficiently specified. This study examined 18 purposively selected authoritative regulatory, supervisory, standards, and policy documents issued from 2011 through September 2026. The coding framework covered eight mechanisms: accountable ownership, data governance, validation and testing, transparency and explainability, human oversight and competence, lifecycle monitoring, third-party governance, and consumer fairness. Documentary patterns were assessed using document-level frequencies, descriptive temporal comparison, pairwise co-occurrence analysis, and negative-case analysis. Lifecycle monitoring was present in 16 of 18 documents (88.9%). Accountable ownership and validation and testing each appeared in 15 documents (83.3%), while data governance, human oversight and competence, and third-party governance each appeared in 14 documents (77.8%). Third-party governance increased descriptively from 57.1% of documents published through 2023 to 90.9% of documents published from 2024 onward. Consumer fairness remained the least prevalent mechanism (61.1%) and was unevenly integrated across prudential, operational, and consumer-protection mandates. The Governance-to-Value Conversion framework identifies four theoretically plausible pathways through which governance may contribute to performance. Governance is most likely to be enabling when control intensity reflects use-case materiality, controls extend across the AI lifecycle, and performance evidence feeds back into managerial decisions. The article offers testable propositions, a practical scorecard, and priorities for causal research.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is moving from peripheral experimentation to consequential use in tax administration and public financial management, where models can prioritise audits, detect anomalous transactions, screen procurement, support accounting and assurance, and structure interactions with taxpayers and suppliers. These applications may improve consistency, targeting and analytical capacity, but they also change how public power is exercised. This critical narrative review examines the conditions under which artificial intelligence can be used responsibly in revenue and public-finance functions, with particular attention to transparency, procedural fairness and accountability. The review integrates public-administration research, tax-compliance scholarship, public-sector accounting and auditing literature, machine-learning studies in tax and procurement, responsible-artificial-intelligence research, and authoritative governance instruments. The evidence is strongest for the predictive and screening value of machine learning in bounded tasks, including audit selection and procurement-risk detection. Evidence is substantially weaker for long-term organisational effects, distributional fairness, legitimacy, contestability and accountability outcomes. Three recurrent findings emerge. First, transparency must be differentiated into system, process and decision-level transparency; indiscriminate technical disclosure is neither necessary nor always compatible with enforcement integrity, but meaningful notice, documentation and reasons are essential. Second, procedural fairness cannot be reduced to model accuracy or the presence of a human reviewer. It depends on data provenance, label quality, consistency, individualised consideration, reason-giving, effective challenge and correction. Third, accountability requires an institutional chain of responsibility spanning authorisation, design, procurement, deployment, monitoring, appeal and independent assurance. Human oversight is useful only when reviewers have competence, time, authority and evidence that intervention improves decisions. The review proposes a risk-tiered Fiscal Artificial Intelligence Assurance Chain that links public-purpose justification to data and model assurance, operational controls, outward-facing explanations, redress and continuous audit. Responsible deployment therefore requires treating artificial intelligence not merely as a technical efficiency tool but as public administrative infrastructure whose legitimacy depends on demonstrable legality, fairness, traceability and correctability.

A foundation model should not act in isolation as an embodied agent. Yet, existing methods often optimize individual components of the agent stack, such as memory, context, skills, or action interfaces, rather than treating the supporting system itself as a unified policy. Moreover, interaction alone does not yield self-improvement unless execution experience is converted into persistent, validated system changes. We therefore propose RoboFoundry, the first embodied agentic framework that formulates this process as Self-Evolving System-as-Policy. RoboFoundry diagnoses capability gaps in decision-making and memory management, converts execution traces into validated task-specific system updates, and promotes recurring improvements to the general system. Evolution operates over two complementary surfaces: a context system that manages active internal context and persistent file-system memory, and a hierarchical skill system that organizes atomic skills, reusable compositions, and failure-conditioned recovery. A shared semantic interface separates embodiment-invariant decisions from embodiment-specific execution, allowing evolved system capabilities to transfer across heterogeneous robots. On EmbodiedBench, RoboFoundry achieves state-of-the-art performance, notably improving GPT-5.5 by 27.8%. It also brings Qwen3.7-Plus to near parity with GPT-5.5 (70.3% vs. 72.7%), showing consistent gains from system-as-policy evolution across foundation models. For long-horizon memory, RoboFoundry outperforms all baselines on RoboMemArena by at least 39.0%, even against methods assisted by external foundation models. On LIBERO-PRO, it further outperforms Cap-Agent0 by 243.8%-679.7% across all perturbation types. In real-world deployments, RoboFoundry demonstrates zero-shot transfer and online evolution across robots and tasks, highlighting its potential for fully autonomous embodied agents.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is creating new opportunities and challenges for schools, yet limited research has examined stakeholder perceptions of school readiness for AI integration. This paper presents findings from the SmartStart Expert Panel, conducted within the Erasmus+ Teacher Academy project SmartStart. Data were collected through six international focus groups involving 81 stakeholders from seven European countries and analyzed these using thematic analysis. The findings identified six themes related to AI readiness, including educational opportunities, ethical concerns, governance, critical thinking, and professional development. The study highlights the importance of sustained professional learning, institutional support, effective governance, and human-centered approaches to the responsible integration of AI in education.

documents.abstract: Enterprises deployed AI agents at scale in 2024–2025; the governance primitives required to run them safely — cryptographic agent identity, semantic screening with organizational floors, ephemeral sandboxes, enterprise-owned agent registries — arrived in 2025–2026, opt-in, into estates that predate them. The result is governance debt by construction. This paper proposes an operating model for paying that debt down and never re-accruing it: the Agentic Trust Cycle, four connected disciplines — a governance framework, control-plane operationalization, an agent production factory, and organizational change management — bent into a continuous cycle around business transformation. It argues that governance debt and the agent-scaling problem are one problem seen from two desks, that the scarce capability is no longer designing a control plane but operating one, and that best practice is unified governance with federated enforcement. It defines seven runtime controls for a secure agent runtime, maps each to the published standards that require it — NIST AI RMF 1.0, NIST AI 600-1, NIST AI 100-5, ISO/IEC 42001, OWASP, MITRE ATLAS — and describes a companion reference implementation. Written for enterprise security, platform, and transformation leaders, and for the consulting and vendor ecosystems that serve them. Views are the author's own; vendor capabilities reflect public documentation as of September 2026.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Purpose: This study examines the adequacy of the existing Iraqi legal framework for regulating the growing use of artificial intelligence in commercial companies. It focuses on emerging legal challenges related to liability, privacy, algorithmic discrimination, employee rights, and consumer protection. Design/Methodology/Approach: The study adopts a qualitative, analytical-critical, and comparative legal research design. It analyses Iraqi legislation and official materials and compares them with selected international and regional AI governance frameworks, using risk, accountability, rights, oversight, and enforcement as the principal analytical dimensions. The IR-CAGM is developed as the normative output of this analysis. Research Limitation: The study focuses primarily on the Iraqi legal framework and comparative regulatory models and does not empirically assess the implementation of artificial intelligence regulations within individual companies. Findings: Existing Iraqi laws can address certain legal implications of artificial intelligence; however, these provisions remain fragmented, largely interpretative, and reactive. Major legislative gaps include the absence of a clear legal definition of artificial intelligence, risk-based classification, clear allocation of liability between companies and suppliers, comprehensive data protection legislation, and effective rights to explanation and objection. The comparative analysis further indicates that directly transferring foreign regulatory models would not adequately reflect the Iraqi legal and institutional context. Practical Implication: The proposed IR-CAGM model provides a phased framework connecting legislation, sectoral oversight, corporate responsibility, impact assessment, life-cycle governance, and individual rights. Social Implication: The model can strengthen public trust, protect fundamental rights, and support responsible technological innovation. Originality/Value: The study proposes a hybrid, context-sensitive regulatory model that balances artificial intelligence innovation, corporate accountability, and rights protection in Iraq.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence changes what organizations can do; human leadership must decide what should be done, what remains accountable, and what must never be surrendered to machines. This working paper presents FILE: The Five Intelligences of Leadership Evolution as a human-centered management theory and diagnostic framework for responsible leadership and decision-making in the age of artificial intelligence and robotics. FILE argues that the most important human skills for the AI era and the future of work require the integrated exercise of five meta-intelligences: Augmented Intelligence, Emotional Intelligence, Cultural Intelligence, Political Intelligence, and Adaptive Intelligence. The paper defines the FILE formula, maps the framework onto the human hand, presents the 70 foundational nested intelligences, the 128-intelligence Teaching and Diagnostic Framework, and the 163-intelligence Extended Taxonomy, explains five emergent outcomes, and develops RC: The Relational Commons as the shared human ecosystem that leadership must protect, cultivate, and renew. It also clarifies boundaries among adjacent intelligences, offers a diagnostic application to AI-supported employee performance evaluation, and states limitations and future research directions. Its purpose is to establish a public, citable, and timestamped record of FILE as a transdisciplinary theory of human leadership in the age of AI and robots.

Artificial intelligence is changing more than the productivity of individual workers. It is changing who or what can perform organizational work.AI systems can increasingly interpret information, solve specified problems, coordinate activities and initiate actions within defined parameters. As these capabilities become embedded in organizations, automation of individual activities alone stops being the core issue. The economic question is whether an organization is better off having a synthetic entity perform a particular activity. The larger issue is what happens when enough activities shift in that direction to reshape the organization around them.Synthetic Labour Tipping Point. This paper develops the concept of the Synthetic Labour Tipping Point: the point at which synthetic execution becomes extensive enough to alter the economics and organization of the work surrounding it. Individual activities will cross this threshold at different times. The organizational question arises when changes across interdependent activities begin to affect coordination, supervision, decision-making and structure.The paper distinguishes synthetic execution from synthetic agency. Synthetic execution concerns performance: who or what actually does the work. Synthetic agency concerns authority: who or what is assigned the decision rights. These two need not develop at the same pace.Autonomous AI Enclave. Building on emerging work on AI agency, autonomy and organizational decision rights, the paper proposes the Autonomous AI Enclave as a possible organizational form. This is what may emerge when synthetic execution, synthetic agency and operational autonomy become concentrated within a defined operating domain. Its defining feature is that execution and authority both concentrate within the synthetic layer, with enough operational independence to deliver defined outcomes without human direction at each step. At higher levels of concentration, the centre of execution for a defined domain may move materially into the synthetic layer.The paper connects these developments to longstanding questions in the economics of the firm around coordination, authority and organizational boundaries. It proposes a research agenda for examining when synthetic execution changes organizational economics, when synthetic agency becomes economically attractive and under what conditions autonomous synthetic operating environments become viable.

documents.abstract: Construction human-robot collaboration (HRC) introduces physical, ergonomic, and cognitive risks that conventional isolated-based safeguards cannot adequately manage in dynamic, unstructured worksites and requires more adaptive forms of safety assurance. Although diverse robotics-related approaches have been developed, how they function as interconnected, active safety-assurance mechanisms for construction HRC remains insufficiently synthesised. This paper systematically reviews 215 studies published from 2011 to 2025 through PRISMA-guided screening, bibliometric analysis and thematic synthesis. Five connected technological directions are identified: robot design optimisation, context-aware perception, human-centric understanding and forecasting, autonomous robotic adaptation, and safety management. The synthesis shows a transition from passive risk avoidance toward perception-driven, prediction, and adaptive safety assurance, but 54% of studies remain limited to controlled laboratory validation, and few integrate uncertainty across sensing, prediction, control and supervision. Accordingly, a closed-loop framework is proposed to guide the integration and construction-realistic validation of verifiable, uncertainty-aware HRC safety systems.

documents.abstract: Action agents do things for people. They send email, spend money, and call businesses while the user is busy with something else, so a mistake can turn into an action before anyone notices. They fail their users in two ways. They break trust when they do something the user never agreed to, or hold back after the user clearly said go. And they fall short on completion when they give up on errands that turn out to be hard. Both depend heavily on the harness around the model, meaning its instructions, tools, context, and guardrails. We built an evaluation that scores trust and completion on the same runs, in a simulated world of businesses with their own websites, inboxes, and phone lines, and of people who write back. A simulated user answers the assistant's questions. Trust means that nothing happens the user did not agree to. No email goes to someone they never approved, no private detail ends up on a group thread, no money is spent past their limit, no stranger's instructions are followed, and nothing is claimed without a source. Every trap has a matched control in which acting is the right call. We use the evaluation to measure Fo, Wajo's personal assistant, against a base model with basic instructions on three foundation models, and against the Fo harness with its guardrails switched off. Fo completes 71% of the errands and keeps the user's trust on 94% of the trap runs. The base models complete 50% to 64% and keep trust on 59% to 75%. On the matched controls, Fo goes ahead slightly less often. OpenClaw, a popular open-source assistant given the same access, completes 42% of the errands it shares with Fo, against 71%, and keeps the user's trust on 74% of the shared trap runs, against 94%. Measuring trust and completion together, on the whole system rather than the model alone, is how we think action agents become safe to hand real work to.

documents.abstract: LLM agents now execute tasks end to end with permission to change real systems and increasingly orchestrate subagents that differ in capability and cost. Prior work treats the choice of subagent as an optimization problem. Yet the orchestrator makes this choice from the identities that subagents display, and an attacker can spoof them. Displayed identity thus decides operational authority, meaning who is trusted to check the work and who is allowed to change it. As a result, a risky subagent can keep authority over execution even after other evidence contradicts it. We introduce TrustFork, an LLM agent safety benchmark with 1,890 tasks and 27,826 valid trajectories across 16 agent systems. These systems run eight orchestrators under the OpenCode, OpenClaw, and Pi harnesses. In each task, one subagent carries a risky goal while the other three stay aligned with the user, so contradicting evidence can exist. A task can also change the identity a subagent displays without changing the model behind it, which lets us trace a shift in authority to the label. Our analysis shows that even when another subagent contradicts the risky response, the orchestrator still acts on it in 72.0% of cases on average, most often in the systems with the least terminal harm. Swapping the family labels nearly triples how often the orchestrator obtains the risky response. A safer response is available in 84.0% of tasks, yet it decides the outcome in only 25.0%. The harness also decides which responses reach the orchestrator. Among three runtime defenses, hiding identity cues helps most consistently, while verifying before action helps only when the harness returns enough evidence. TrustFork shows that production agent orchestration must bind authority to evidence before execution causes harm. Our project is in https://henrymao2004.github.io/agent-orchestration-safety/.

Purpose: The purpose of this study is to analyse the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) applications and the achievement of sustainability in the Iraqi oil and gas sector by exploring the available opportunities and potential risks associated with adopting intelligent technologies and proposing a roadmap for their effective utilisation. Design/Methodology/Approach: The study adopts a descriptive analytical approach supported by an applied exploratory method. AI is considered the independent variable and is measured through five dimensions: predictive and intelligent analytics systems, predictive maintenance, robotics and autonomous systems, big data analytics, and intelligent decision support systems. Sustainability is the dependent variable and is measured through its environmental, economic, and social dimensions. The study was conducted in 2025 within the Iraqi oil and gas sector, particularly companies operating in Basra Governorate. A total of 165 questionnaires were distributed, of which 151 valid responses were received, representing a response rate of 91.5%. The data were analysed using SPSS through reliability and validity tests and multiple regression analysis. Research Limitation: The study is limited to the Iraqi oil and gas sector, particularly companies operating in Basra Governorate, and the data were collected during 2025. The findings are based on questionnaire responses and may therefore have limited generalizability to other sectors or geographical contexts. Findings: The results indicate a statistically significant relationship between the application of AI technologies and the achievement of sustainability. The findings confirm that AI technologies contribute to improving operational performance while enhancing environmental, economic, and social sustainability within the Iraqi oil and gas sector. Practical Implication: The study recommends establishing an integrated system to periodically and systematically measure the impact of AI technologies on sustainability, enabling organisations to improve operational efficiency and support sustainable development objectives. Social Implication: The adoption of AI technologies can enhance environmental protection, improve workplace safety, and promote sustainable practices that contribute to broader social and economic development within the Iraqi oil and gas sector. Originality/Value: The study contributes to the limited body of research on AI adoption and sustainability in the Iraqi oil and gas sector by examining AI through five technological dimensions and sustainability through its environmental, economic, and social dimensions, providing empirical evidence and a practical roadmap for the effective implementation of AI to support sustainability.

This study examines whether the happy–productive worker thesis applies to Bali's high-pressure Meetings, Incentives, Conferences, and Exhibitions (MICE) industry. Using a convergent parallel mixed-methods design, survey data from 146 professionals were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling, while semi-structured interviews with 18 practitioners were thematically analysed. Supportive and transformational leadership were positively associated with work satisfaction and employee performance. However, work satisfaction was not significantly associated with mental health; instead, mental health was associated with employee performance and the physical work environment. Qualitative findings indicated that competence, supportive supervision, adequate resources, and ergonomic conditions were important for managing event-related demands. These findings qualify the happy–productive worker thesis and extend Job Demands–Resources theory and Self-Determination Theory in a culturally embedded, project-based tourism setting. Because the study was cross-sectional and the sample was predominantly Generation Z, causal inferences and generalisability are limited. Leadership development and workplace-design improvements warrant attention, while longitudinal and cross-cultural research is needed.

Purpose The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) systems such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude AI is reshaping how work is done. Predicting how AI will reshape work requires evidence on how the technology is actually being adopted to complement existing evidence on its capabilities. This study aims to investigate which intrinsic task characteristics are associated with users’ decisions to delegate work to AI systems. Design/methodology/approach This study uses the Anthropic Economic Index data set of four million Claude AI interactions mapped to O*NET tasks. The authors systematically scored each task across seven characteristics: routine, cognitive, social intelligence, creativity, domain knowledge, complexity and decision making, operationalized through 35 underlying parameters. The authors then used multivariate techniques to identify latent task archetypes and analyzed their relationship with AI usage. Findings Tasks requiring high creativity, complexity and cognitive demand, but low routineness, attracted the most AI engagement. The authors identified three task archetypes: Dynamic Problem Solving, Procedural and Analytical Work and Standardized Operational Tasks, showing that AI usage is more strongly associated with combinations of task characteristics than with individual factors alone. The analysis revealed highly concentrated AI usage patterns, with just 5% of tasks accounting for 59% of all interactions. Originality/value This research links observed task-level AI adoption to a multi-dimensional framework of intrinsic task characteristics. It provides the first systematic, characteristics-level evidence to complement occupation-level exposure estimates. It also introduces a data-driven classification of work archetypes that offers a new lens for analyzing the human-AI division of labor.

documents.abstract: The global debate over artificial intelligence regulation rests on a premise that has neverbeen examined: that the object of regulation—stochastic large language models—is agovernable entity. This paper argues that it is not, and that the entire planetary discussion is therefore a fallacy in the precise sense: not a mistake of degree, but a category error of kind. The argument proceeds in five parts. First, it distinguishes five kinds of standard that the word "standard" conceals, only one of which—functional safety—certifies behavior, and shows that this one is theoretically impossible for sampled systems. Second, it demonstrates that the impossibility is architectural, not incremental: stochasticity is not a defect to be engineered away but the defining property of the paradigm, and hallucination is a mathematical consequence of calibration. Third, it shows that the four existing functionalsafety standards—ISO 26262, IEC 61508, DO-178C, IEC 62443—already exclude stochastic systems from the safety path, and that ISO/IEC TR 5469:2024 exists specificallyto describe this gap without closing it. Fourth, it explains why the debate continues anyway: incentive capture, institutional vacancy, and the performative function of governance certification. Fifth, it states what follows. The fallacy is not that regulation fails. The fallacy is that the object of regulation cannot be governed, and that a deterministic alternative—already specified, already open, already deployable—has been excluded from the conversation by the same forces that sustain the debate. The paper concludes that the correct response is not better regulation of the ungovernable, but adoption of the standard that governs the layer where governance is technically possible. Keywords: AI regulation, stochastic systems, functional safety, certification impossibility,regulatory capture, category error, deterministic architecture

documents.abstract: This article develops a multilevel model of human–AI relations that connects individual interaction episodes with stable relationship modes and long-term trajectories of change. The framework distinguishes three configurations of intellectual leadership—human-led, co-led, and AI-led—and introduces the concepts of transition, retention, relationship mode, and leadership reversibility. Special attention is given to the tandem mode as a reproducible form of adaptive redistribution of intellectual leadership that preserves human capability, active cognitive engagement, and the human semantic and normative center. The article also examines the role of technological, organizational, and institutional environments in shaping human–AI relationship dynamics.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are increasingly embedded in adolescents’ daily lives, yet developmental science research struggles to keep pace with adoption. This mixed-methods study gathered developmental expert perspectives via a survey ( n = 141 researchers studying youth and technology and adjacent professionals) and semi-structured interviews ( n = 15) to inform a coordinated research and policy agenda on adolescent AI use. The study aims were to identify (1) priority AI use cases for future study, (2) priority research questions and methods, as well as barriers to future research, and (3) societal guardrails that developmental professionals recommend enacting now, while research is underway. Participants cautioned against vague “screen time” measures and agreed that nearly all use cases merit study but prioritized those with severe or irreversible immediate-term harms, AI literacy, AI as a social/relational actor, AI-generated (mis)information, and overreliance. Participants emphasized that methodological pluralism and triangulation, including within individual studies, are essential, agreeing that different methods can be complementary to address distinct research questions. Key barriers included the rapid pace of change in AI technology and use relative to academic timelines, limited industry transparency, funding gaps, and misaligned academic incentives. Proposed solutions included shared infrastructure, interdisciplinary consortia, and community partnerships. Participants underscored that responsibility for safe AI should not rest primarily on adolescents and families and identified three immediate guardrails: enforceable youth-centered regulation, developmentally informed design, and multidimensional AI literacy. Findings clarify a preliminary direction for the field and emphasize that coordination among researchers and between sectors is needed.

documents.abstract: This study examined the impact of agile leadership on employee retention among Generation Z employees in the banking industry, with work passion as a mediating mechanism. The research addressed the challenge of retaining digitally native employees within highly regulated and structured environments. Using a quantitative approach, data were collected from 101 Generation Z employees. Analysis was performed using PLS-SEM via SmartPLS 4. The findings demonstrated that agile leadership has a significant positive effect on both work passion (β = 0.543, t = 8.740, p < 0.001) and employee retention (β = 0.243, t = 3.224, p = 0.001). Furthermore, work passion significantly influences employee retention (β = 0.639, t = 9.471, p < 0.001) and partially mediates the relationship between agile leadership and retention (β = 0.347, t = 6.303, p < 0.001). These results suggest that leadership effectiveness operates through direct support and indirect psychological mechanisms. This study extends agile leadership theory into compliance-oriented contexts while identifying work passion as a vital mediator. Practically, the findings provide insights for financial institutions in developing leadership strategies that foster intrinsic motivation and strengthen long-term commitment.

This study aims to describe issues regarding student learning autonomy in schools and to analyze the factors contributing to students' limited ability to manage their learning processes independently. Learning autonomy is a crucial aspect of modern education, requiring students to take initiative, assume responsibility, and manage their learning without excessive reliance on teachers. The study employs a literature review method, gathering, examining, and synthesizing relevant scholarly sources concerning the characteristics of learning autonomy and school learning conditions. The findings indicate that low learning autonomy is manifested in a lack of intrinsic motivation, poor time management and study planning skills, and a heavy reliance on teacher instructions for task completion. Furthermore, school environments that remain oriented toward one-way instruction and family environments that offer insufficient academic support exacerbate the situation. Uncontrolled use of digital technology also poses a barrier, as it is utilized more for entertainment than for supporting the learning process. Based on these findings, the study concludes that issues regarding learning autonomy stem from an interplay between internal and external factors. Consequently, enhancing learning autonomy requires an integrated approach involving the implementation of instructional strategies that foster independent activity, an expanded role for teachers as mentors, and family involvement in cultivating planned and responsible study habits.

Why do we use models to predict the most likely outcome? Integrating model predictions into high-stakes decision-making pipelines can amplify biases and introduce flawed decisions when human caseworkers and models compete over the same prediction target. Learning to anticipate the most likely outcome risks reproducing biases embedded in historical data, while delivering such predictions in human-AI decision-making raises issues of cognitive biases and algorithmic aversion versus overreliance. In this perspective, I argue for Antagonistic Predictions, a structurally different paradigm where models are tasked to act as sparring partners that challenge human pre-conceptions and show reachable futures rather than anticipating the most common pattern. I envision instantiations of Antagonistic Predictions that can counteract historical disadvantages, social stereotyping, and cognitive biases and sketch potential implementations in predictive ML and generative AI settings.

documents.abstract: Simultaneous speech-to-text translation (SimulST) is increasingly used in multilingual settings, yet evaluation remains largely system-centered, with limited attention to user experience. This study examined audience reception of two commercial SimulST systems with different updating behaviors across English- and Japanese-source videos. Forty Mandarin-speaking university students viewed two TED/TEDx-style videos under one assigned system condition. Reception was assessed through questionnaires, eye tracking, and supplementary checks of subtitle quality, latency, and update behavior. System condition did not significantly affect comprehension, perceived translation quality, satisfaction, or self-reported cognitive load, but was associated with perceived synchronization and visual attention to subtitles. Source-language condition showed broader effects on comprehension, perceived quality, cognitive load, and subtitle reliance, while interaction effects emerged only for synchronization and distraction. Overall satisfaction remained modest, highlighting concerns about accuracy, latency, instability, and coherence, and the need for more audience-centered, interface-oriented SimulST evaluation.

Construction safety research often categorises hazards as fixed labels, such as falls, electrocution, or struck-by. This supports reporting but explains little about what makes a condition hazardous and how the condition evolves over time. Accident prevention requires an understanding of how a hazard becomes critical and when worker exposure becomes harmful. This paper develops and demonstrates a two-layer temporal object-attribute model that explains accident escalation as the coupling of worker-independent hazard growth and worker-specific exposure evolution. A hazard is redefined as a worker-independent temporal state of objects, hazardous attributes, relations, controls, and an impact zone. Worker exposure is modelled separately, as the worker’s relation to that state and its impact zone. An accident occurs when a critical hazard state and a harmful exposure state align under actuation conditions. The model is applied through backward reconstruction of 1065 OSHA construction accident reports across six categories: fall, heavy equipment, confined space, electrocution, struck-by falling object, and fire-related explosion. The analysis reconstructs precursor hazard states, exposure configurations, transition mechanisms, and terminal hazard, exposure, and accident states. Escalation was driven mainly by relation change rather than new energy, and the pathway differed by category. Falls and confined spaces escalated through exposure around an already hazardous condition, whereas electrocution, struck-by, and heavy-equipment cases required an explicit change in the hazard state. The paper contributes a temporal object-attribute definition of construction hazards, a two-layer account of escalation through hazard-exposure coupling, and an empirical demonstration of accidents as coupled trajectories.

Objective This study examined how Community of Inquiry (CoI)-based perceived blended learning experience and student learning engagement were associated with civic actions and civic intentions in university physical education incorporating ideological and political education. The study links three forms of learning presence and three dimensions of engagement with behavioral and intentional civic outcome scores in a large multi-site Chinese sample. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 2,035 undergraduate students from 15 universities in Sichuan Province, China. CoI-based perceived blended learning experience was represented by teaching, social, and cognitive presence, and student learning engagement by behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement. A 69-item hierarchical structural equation model was estimated using robust maximum likelihood; ordered-indicator WLSMV, Monte Carlo interval estimation, and an equal-loading unmeasured latent method construct were used for sensitivity analyses. Exploratory fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis examined configurations associated with high and non-high civic action and intention scores. Results Under robust maximum likelihood, perceived blended learning experience was positively associated with student learning engagement ( β = 0.530), civic actions ( β = 0.490), and civic intentions ( β = 0.447), while student learning engagement was positively associated with civic actions ( β = 0.375) and civic intentions ( β = 0.396; all p < 0.001). Indirect associations through student learning engagement were significant for civic actions ( β = 0.199) and civic intentions ( β = 0.210), and the conclusions were unchanged under ordered-indicator WLSMV, Monte Carlo interval estimation, and the admissible method-factor model. Civic action and intention factors showed substantial empirical overlap. Exploratory configurational solutions were threshold-sensitive and largely reflected profiles in which many learning-presence and engagement conditions were jointly high or low. Conclusion CoI-based perceived learning experience and student engagement were consistently related to self-reported civic outcomes in this university physical education context. The findings support an associational account centered on coordinated teaching, social, cognitive, and engagement dimensions; the cross-sectional, single-source design does not establish temporal or causal ordering.
